ROYAL OBSERVATORY · GREENWICH, ENGLAND
THE REFERENCE BEHIND THE GRAPHIC

A bearing, on a sphere.

The white line passes through your point in the local direction of the shortest great-circle route to the Royal Observatory. That direction is projected onto this flat, orthographic view. It need not pass through the Observatory’s on-screen marker: a straight tangent and a curved surface route are different geometries.

Historic celestial navigation solves a spherical triangle to determine a celestial body’s altitude and azimuth. Marine chronometers supplied Greenwich time for finding longitude. This tool uses related spherical geometry to find a terrestrial bearing; it does not simulate a sextant sight or a celestial line of position.

The target is the historic Airy Transit Circle, approximately 51.477806° N, 0.001472° W in modern geographic coordinates. The historic Greenwich meridian lies about 102 metres west of GPS zero longitude.

Rotate and tilt the view to explore both hemispheres. A point behind the globe is hidden until brought back into view. At Greenwich and its antipode the bearing is undefined, so the line is hidden. At the rim a bearing aimed directly into the screen has no visible line direction.

Line length is a percentage of the globe’s diameter. Point size and stroke thickness use a 1,000-unit artwork canvas. Distance uses the historic spherical convention of 60 nautical miles per degree. At an exact pole, the bearing readout uses the point’s stored longitude as its north reference.
